title: What is React?

blocks.text: React is an open-source JavaScript library, created by Meta (Facebook), for building user interfaces out of reusable pieces called components. It is "declarative": you describe what the UI should look like for a given state, and React works out how to update the browser DOM efficiently when that state changes.
React focuses only on the view layer. Routing, data fetching and global state are handled by separate libraries or by frameworks built on React such as Next.js or React Router.
Interview tip: In interviews, mention the three ideas that define React: components, declarative rendering, and one-way data flow.

title: What are the main features of React?

blocks.text: • Component-based architecture: UIs are built from small, reusable, self-contained components.
• JSX: an HTML-like syntax extension that makes component markup easy to read.
• Virtual DOM and reconciliation: React compares UI trees and applies only the minimal DOM changes needed.
• One-way data flow: data moves from parent to child through props, which makes behaviour predictable.
• Hooks: functions like useState and useEffect that give function components state and lifecycle features.
• Rich ecosystem and cross-platform support (React Native for mobile apps).

title: What is JSX?

blocks.text: JSX (JavaScript XML) is a syntax extension that lets you write HTML-like markup inside JavaScript. Browsers cannot run JSX directly; a compiler such as Babel, SWC or esbuild converts it into ordinary function calls (React.createElement or the newer jsx() runtime).
Because JSX is JavaScript, you can embed any expression inside curly braces, and JSX itself is an expression you can store in variables or return from functions.
Interview tip: Use className instead of class, and htmlFor instead of for, because class and for are reserved words in JavaScript.

title: Can you write React without JSX?

blocks.text: Yes. JSX is only syntactic sugar for React.createElement(type, props, ...children). Writing createElement by hand works but becomes hard to read for nested markup, which is why almost every project uses JSX.

title: What is the Virtual DOM?

blocks.text: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight in-memory JavaScript representation of the real DOM. When state changes, React builds a new virtual tree, compares it with the previous one (a process called "diffing"), and then applies only the changed parts to the real DOM.

Real DOM operations are comparatively slow because they can trigger layout and repaint. Batching and minimizing these operations keeps updates efficient while letting developers write code as if the whole UI re-renders every time.

title: What is the difference between the Real DOM and the Virtual DOM?

blocks.text: • The Real DOM is the browser's actual document tree; the Virtual DOM is a plain JavaScript object copy of it kept by React.
• Updating the Real DOM directly can be slow and cause reflows; updating the Virtual DOM is cheap because it is just object manipulation.
• The Real DOM updates immediately on every change; React batches Virtual DOM changes and commits the minimal difference.
• Developers manipulate the Real DOM imperatively (document.querySelector...); with the Virtual DOM you describe the UI declaratively.

title: What is reconciliation in React?

blocks.text: Reconciliation is the algorithm React uses to compare the new element tree with the previous one and decide what DOM changes are required. It relies on two heuristics that make diffing O(n) instead of O(n^3):
• Elements of different types produce completely different trees (e.g. changing a div to a section unmounts the old subtree).
• Keys on list children tell React which items are stable across renders.

title: What is React Fiber?

blocks.text: Fiber is the reconciliation engine introduced in React 16. It breaks rendering work into small units ("fibers") that can be paused, resumed, prioritized or discarded. This makes features like concurrent rendering, transitions, Suspense and time-slicing possible.

Before Fiber, rendering was synchronous and could block the main thread on large trees. With Fiber, React can interrupt low-priority work (like rendering a long filtered list) to handle urgent work (like typing in an input).

title: What are components in React?

blocks.text: Components are independent, reusable building blocks of a React UI. Each component is a JavaScript function (or class) that accepts inputs called props and returns React elements describing what should appear on screen. Component names must start with a capital letter so JSX can distinguish them from HTML tags.

title: What is the difference between functional and class components?

blocks.text: Functional components are plain functions that receive props and return JSX; with Hooks they can hold state and run side effects. Class components extend React.Component, keep state in this.state, and use lifecycle methods such as componentDidMount.

Function components are now the recommended approach: they are shorter, avoid confusion with "this", and make logic reuse easy through custom hooks. Class components are still supported and required only for error boundaries.

title: What are props in React?

blocks.text: Props (short for properties) are read-only inputs passed from a parent component to a child, similar to function arguments. They let you configure and reuse components with different data. A component must never modify its own props; to change data it uses state or asks the parent to change it via a callback prop.

title: What is state in React?

blocks.text: State is data owned by a component that can change over time. When state is updated through its setter function, React re-renders the component so the UI reflects the new values. Unlike props, state is private and managed inside the component.
Interview tip: Store in state only the data that changes and affects rendering; derive everything else during render.

title: What is the difference between state and props?

blocks.text: • Ownership: props are passed in by the parent; state is created and managed inside the component.
• Mutability: props are read-only for the receiving component; state can be updated with its setter.
• Purpose: props configure a component; state tracks values that change through interaction or time.
• Flow: changing a parent's state can change the props its children receive.

title: Why should we not update state directly?

blocks.text: Mutating state directly (e.g. state.count = 5 or array.push in place) does not tell React that anything changed, so no re-render happens. It also breaks optimizations such as React.memo and useMemo, which rely on reference comparisons to detect changes. Always call the setter with a new value or new object/array.

title: What is the children prop?

blocks.text: children is a special prop containing whatever you place between a component's opening and closing tags. It allows building wrapper or layout components (cards, modals, layouts) that do not need to know their content in advance.

title: What are React Fragments?

blocks.text: Fragments let a component return multiple elements without adding an extra DOM node. This keeps markup clean and avoids breaking layouts such as tables or flex containers. Use the short syntax <>...</>, or <React.Fragment key={...}> when you need a key in a list.

title: What are keys and why are they important in lists?

blocks.text: Keys are special string or number attributes that help React identify which list items have changed, been added or been removed. A stable key lets React reuse the existing DOM node and component state for the same item across renders. Without proper keys, React may mismatch items, causing wrong state, lost input focus or unnecessary re-renders.
Interview tip: Keys only need to be unique among siblings, not globally.

title: Why is using the array index as a key a bad idea?

blocks.text: If the list can be reordered, filtered, or have items inserted at the start, the index of each item changes. React then associates the old component state with the wrong item. This causes bugs like a checkbox staying checked on the wrong row or input text jumping between items. Index keys are acceptable only for static lists that never change order.

title: How do you conditionally render elements in React?

blocks.text: React uses normal JavaScript for conditions. Common patterns include if/else with early return, the ternary operator, logical && and returning null to render nothing.
Interview tip: Beware of {count && <List />} when count is 0; React renders the 0. Use {count > 0 && <List />}.

title: How do you render a list in React?

blocks.text: Use the array map() method to transform data into an array of elements, giving each a unique key. You can combine filter(), sort() and map() to prepare the data before rendering.

title: How do you handle events in React?

blocks.text: React events use camelCase names (onClick, onChange, onSubmit) and you pass a function, not a string. React wraps native events in a SyntheticEvent with the same interface across browsers. Call e.preventDefault() explicitly to stop default behaviour; returning false does not work.

title: What are synthetic events in React?

blocks.text: A SyntheticEvent is React's cross-browser wrapper around the browser's native event. It exposes the same API (target, preventDefault, stopPropagation) and behaves consistently across browsers. Since React 17, events are attached to the root container instead of the document, and event pooling has been removed, so you can safely access the event asynchronously. The native event is available as e.nativeEvent.

title: What are controlled components?

blocks.text: A controlled component is a form element whose value is driven by React state. The value comes from state and every change goes through an onChange handler that updates state. This makes the React state the "single source of truth", enabling instant validation, formatting and conditional disabling.

title: What are uncontrolled components?

blocks.text: In an uncontrolled component, the DOM itself keeps the form value, and React reads it when needed, usually via a ref. You use defaultValue (or defaultChecked) to set the initial value. This is simpler for basic forms, file inputs, or integrating non-React code, but gives less control over each keystroke.

title: What is the difference between controlled and uncontrolled components?

blocks.text: • Data source: controlled uses React state; uncontrolled uses the DOM.
• Access: controlled reads from state; uncontrolled reads via refs (or FormData).
• Initial value: controlled uses value; uncontrolled uses defaultValue.
• Validation: controlled supports validation on every keystroke; uncontrolled usually validates on submit.
• Re-renders: controlled re-renders on every change; uncontrolled does not.
Libraries like React Hook Form use mostly uncontrolled inputs for performance, while small forms often use controlled inputs for simplicity.

<input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />  // controlled
<input defaultValue="Guest" ref={nameRef} />                     // uncontrolled

title: What is lifting state up?

blocks.text: When two or more sibling components need the same changing data, you move ("lift") that state to their closest common parent. The parent owns the state and passes it down as props, along with callbacks to change it. This keeps components in sync with a single source of truth.

title: What is one-way data binding in React?

blocks.text: React uses unidirectional data flow: data flows down from parent to child through props, and changes flow up only through callback functions. A child cannot directly change its parent's data. This makes it easy to trace where data comes from and why the UI changed, compared with two-way binding frameworks.

title: What is prop drilling and how can you avoid it?

blocks.text: Prop drilling is passing props through several intermediate components that don't use them, just to reach a deeply nested child. It makes code verbose and fragile. Solutions include the Context API, component composition (passing JSX as children), and state management libraries such as Redux or Zustand.

title: What are default props and how do you set them?

blocks.text: Default props provide fallback values when a parent does not pass a prop. In function components, the modern way is JavaScript default parameters in destructuring. The older Component.defaultProps is deprecated for function components in React 19.

title: What is PropTypes?

blocks.text: PropTypes is a runtime type-checking library (prop-types package) that warns in development when a component receives props of the wrong type. It has largely been replaced by TypeScript, which catches errors at compile time; React 19 no longer checks propTypes on function components.

title: How do you apply styles in React?

blocks.text: • Plain CSS files imported into components, using className.
• Inline styles with a JavaScript object (camelCased properties).
• CSS Modules for locally scoped class names.
• CSS-in-JS libraries such as styled-components or Emotion.
• Utility-first frameworks such as Tailwind CSS.

title: What are CSS Modules?

blocks.text: CSS Modules are CSS files where every class name is scoped locally to the component by default. The build tool renames classes to unique names (e.g. Button_primary__x7f2), preventing collisions between components. Files are usually named *.module.css.

title: What is the difference between an Element and a Component?

blocks.text: A React element is a plain, immutable object describing what should appear on screen, e.g. { type: "h1", props: {...} }. A component is a function or class that returns elements. Components are blueprints; elements are the instances of output React uses to build the tree.

title: What is React.StrictMode?

blocks.text: StrictMode is a development-only wrapper that highlights potential problems. It renders nothing visible and has no effect in production. In development it double-invokes component bodies, state initializers and effects (mount, unmount, mount) to surface impure rendering and missing effect cleanup, and warns about deprecated APIs.
Interview tip: If you see an effect running twice in development, it is usually StrictMode checking that your cleanup works correctly.

title: What is the difference between createRoot and ReactDOM.render?

blocks.text: ReactDOM.render was the legacy API (React 17 and earlier) and has been removed in React 19. createRoot (from react-dom/client, introduced in React 18) creates a root that enables concurrent features like automatic batching, transitions and Suspense streaming.

title: What is a pure component in React?

blocks.text: A pure component always renders the same output for the same props and state and has no side effects during rendering. React expects all components to be pure during render. In class components, React.PureComponent automatically skips re-rendering if props and state are shallowly equal; the function-component equivalent is React.memo.

title: Why must React components be pure functions during rendering?

blocks.text: React may render a component multiple times, pause rendering, or discard results (especially with concurrent features). If rendering changes external variables, makes network calls, or mutates props, these repeated renders produce bugs. Side effects belong in event handlers or useEffect, not in the render body.

title: How does React render HTML strings safely, and what is dangerouslySetInnerHTML?

blocks.text: By default React escapes all values embedded in JSX, which protects against cross-site scripting (XSS). If you truly need to insert raw HTML (e.g. from a CMS), use dangerouslySetInnerHTML with an object { __html: string }. The awkward name is a deliberate warning; always sanitize the HTML first (for example with DOMPurify).

title: How do you pass data from child to parent?

blocks.text: Pass a callback function from the parent to the child as a prop. The child calls that function with data, and the parent updates its state.

title: How do you share data between sibling components?

blocks.text: Siblings do not talk directly. Lift the shared state to their common parent and pass it down, or use Context or a global store if they are far apart in the tree.

title: Why must component names start with a capital letter?

blocks.text: JSX treats lowercase tags as built-in DOM elements (div, span) and capitalized tags as references to components. If you name a component in lowercase, React will try to create an unknown HTML element instead of calling your function.

title: How do you render a component dynamically based on a string?

blocks.text: Create a map from strings to components, look up the component, assign it to a capitalized variable, and render it. This is useful for CMS-driven pages, dashboards and form builders.

title: What is the spread operator used for with props?

blocks.text: The spread syntax {...obj} passes every property of an object as individual props. It is handy for forwarding props to a child or a native element, but overusing it can pass unexpected attributes to the DOM. Combine it with rest destructuring to separate custom props from the rest.

title: What is the difference between React and ReactDOM?

blocks.text: The react package contains the core: components, hooks, createElement, context. It is platform-independent. react-dom contains the renderer for web browsers: createRoot, portals, flushSync, and form actions. Other renderers include React Native (mobile) and react-three-fiber (3D).

import { useState } from "react";              // core
import { createRoot } from "react-dom/client"; // browser renderer
import { createPortal } from "react-dom";      // browser-only feature

title: Is React a library or a framework?

blocks.text: React itself is a library focused on rendering UI. It does not prescribe routing, data fetching, bundling or folder structure. However, the React team now recommends starting new apps with a framework built on React (Next.js, React Router v7 framework mode, Expo for native) that supplies these missing pieces. So in interviews, say "React is a UI library; frameworks like Next.js are built on top of it."

# Plain React with a build tool
npm create vite@latest my-app -- --template react
# Full-stack React framework
npx create-next-app@latest my-app

title: What are the advantages and limitations of React?

blocks.text: Advantages:
• Reusable components and a large ecosystem.
• Efficient updates through the Virtual DOM and concurrent rendering.
• Strong community, tooling (DevTools) and React Native for mobile.
• Easy to learn core concepts; works well with TypeScript.
Limitations:
• Only the view layer; you must choose routing, state and data libraries.
• Fast-moving ecosystem with frequent new patterns.
• JSX and build tooling add a learning curve.
• Client-side-only apps need extra work for SEO (solved by SSR frameworks).

title: What is create-react-app and what do people use now?

blocks.text: Create React App (CRA) was the official tool for bootstrapping single-page React apps with zero config. It was deprecated in February 2025 because of slow builds and lack of modern features. Today developers use Vite for client-side apps, or frameworks such as Next.js and React Router for full-stack apps with routing, SSR and data loading.

npm create vite@latest shop -- --template react-ts
cd shop && npm install && npm run dev

title: How do you write comments in JSX?

blocks.text: Inside JSX, comments must be wrapped in curly braces as JavaScript block comments. Outside JSX, normal // and /* */ comments work.

title: Why must JSX return a single root element?

blocks.text: A component returns one value, and JSX compiles to a single createElement call, so you cannot return two sibling elements without wrapping them. Use a Fragment to group siblings without adding extra DOM nodes.

title: How do you handle forms with multiple inputs using a single handler?

blocks.text: Give each input a name attribute matching a key in a state object, then use computed property names to update the right field.

title: What are Hooks in React?

blocks.text: Hooks are functions, introduced in React 16.8, that let function components use state, side effects, context, refs and other React features without writing classes. Built-in hooks include useState, useEffect, useContext, useRef, useMemo, useCallback, useReducer, useId, useTransition, useDeferredValue, and in React 19, use, useActionState, useFormStatus and useOptimistic. You can also write your own custom hooks to reuse logic.

title: What are the Rules of Hooks?

blocks.text: • Only call hooks at the top level of a component or custom hook. Never call them inside loops, conditions, nested functions or after an early return.
• Only call hooks from React function components or custom hooks, not from regular JavaScript functions or class components.
React identifies each hook by its call order. If the order changes between renders, React assigns state to the wrong hook. The eslint-plugin-react-hooks package enforces these rules.
Interview tip: The new use() hook is an exception: it can be called inside conditions.

title: How does useState work?

blocks.text: useState(initialValue) returns an array of two items: the current state value and a setter function. Calling the setter schedules a re-render with the new value. The initial value is used only on the first render.

title: What is a functional (updater) state update and when should you use it?

blocks.text: Passing a function to the setter, setCount(prev => prev + 1), tells React to compute the new state from the latest value. Use it whenever the new state depends on the previous state, especially when updating several times in one event or inside closures such as timers, where the captured value may be stale.

title: Is setState synchronous or asynchronous?

blocks.text: State updates are not applied immediately. Calling a setter schedules an update, and React batches multiple updates and re-renders afterwards. Therefore reading the state variable right after setting it still gives the old value for the current render. Use the next render, an effect, or the updater form to work with the new value.

title: What is lazy initialization in useState?

blocks.text: If the initial state is expensive to compute (e.g. reading localStorage or parsing large data), pass a function instead of a value. React calls it only on the first render. Passing the result directly would recompute it on every render even though it's ignored.

title: What is automatic batching?

blocks.text: Batching means React groups multiple state updates into a single re-render for performance. Before React 18, batching only happened inside React event handlers. Since React 18 with createRoot, updates are automatically batched everywhere: in promises, setTimeout, native event handlers and more. You can opt out with flushSync from react-dom when you need the DOM updated immediately.

title: How does useEffect work?

blocks.text: useEffect(setup, dependencies) runs side effects after React has committed changes to the screen. Typical effects include subscriptions, timers, manual DOM work and synchronizing with external systems. The setup function can return a cleanup function, which React calls before re-running the effect and when the component unmounts.

title: Explain the dependency array in useEffect.

blocks.text: • No array: the effect runs after every render.
• Empty array []: the effect runs only after the first render (mount) and cleans up on unmount.
• [a, b]: the effect runs after the first render and whenever a or b changes (compared with Object.is).

Every reactive value used inside the effect (props, state, functions defined in the component) should be listed; the exhaustive-deps lint rule helps with this. Missing dependencies cause stale values.

title: What is the cleanup function in useEffect and why is it important?

blocks.text: The cleanup function undoes what the effect set up: removing event listeners, clearing timers, cancelling requests or closing connections. React runs it before the effect re-runs with new dependencies and when the component unmounts. Without cleanup you get memory leaks, duplicate subscriptions and state updates on unmounted components.

title: How do you fetch data with useEffect correctly?

blocks.text: Start the request in an effect, store the result in state, and handle loading and error states. Use AbortController (or an ignore flag) in the cleanup to avoid race conditions when the dependency changes quickly. In production apps, prefer a data library (TanStack Query, SWR) or a framework's loaders, which add caching and deduplication.

title: Why can't the useEffect callback be async?

blocks.text: An async function always returns a Promise, but React expects the effect to return either nothing or a cleanup function. Returning a Promise breaks cleanup. Instead, define an async function inside the effect and call it.

title: What is the difference between useEffect and useLayoutEffect?

blocks.text: useEffect runs asynchronously after the browser has painted, so it does not block visual updates. useLayoutEffect runs synchronously after DOM mutations but before the browser paints. Use useLayoutEffect only when you must measure layout and update synchronously to prevent flicker, such as positioning a tooltip. Overusing it hurts performance.

title: What is useInsertionEffect?

blocks.text: useInsertionEffect fires before React makes any DOM changes and before layout effects. It is intended only for CSS-in-JS library authors to inject style tags so that styles exist before layout is read. Application code should almost never use it.

title: What does useRef do?

blocks.text: useRef(initialValue) returns a mutable object { current: initialValue } that persists across renders. Changing ref.current does not trigger a re-render. It has two main uses: getting direct access to DOM nodes, and storing mutable values such as timer IDs or previous values.

title: What is the difference between useRef and useState?

blocks.text: • useState triggers a re-render when updated; useRef does not.
• State values are snapshots per render; ref.current always holds the latest value and can be changed anytime.
• Use state for data shown in the UI; use refs for values needed by event handlers or effects but not for rendering (IDs, DOM nodes, previous values).
• Do not read or write ref.current during rendering (except lazy init), because it makes components unpredictable.

title: How do you store the previous value of a prop or state?

blocks.text: One common approach uses a ref updated in an effect, so it holds the value from the previous render. The React docs also suggest storing the previous value in state and comparing during render when you need to react to changes.

title: What is forwardRef and how have refs changed in React 19?

blocks.text: Refs normally cannot be passed to function components like regular props. forwardRef wrapped a component so it received a ref as a second argument and could attach it to an inner DOM element. In React 19, ref is available as a normal prop for function components, so forwardRef is no longer needed (it is being deprecated).

title: What is useImperativeHandle?

blocks.text: useImperativeHandle customizes what a parent receives when it holds a ref to your component. Instead of exposing the whole DOM node, you expose a limited API (such as focus or scrollToTop). It is used with ref props (or forwardRef in older versions).

title: What are callback refs?

blocks.text: Instead of a ref object, you can pass a function to the ref attribute. React calls it with the DOM node when it is attached and (in React 19) calls the returned cleanup when detached; in older versions it calls the function with null. Callback refs are useful for measuring nodes when they appear, or managing a dynamic list of refs.

title: What does useContext do?

blocks.text: useContext(SomeContext) reads the current value of a context from the nearest Provider above the component. When the provider's value changes, every component using that context re-renders. It eliminates prop drilling for values like theme, auth user, or language.
Interview tip: In React 19 you can render <ThemeContext value={theme}> directly instead of <ThemeContext.Provider>.

title: What does useReducer do and when should you use it over useState?

blocks.text: useReducer(reducer, initialState) manages state through a reducer function (state, action) => newState, and returns [state, dispatch]. Prefer it when state has several related fields, when the next state depends on complex logic, or when many event handlers update the state in different ways. It centralizes update logic and makes it easy to test.

title: How can you combine useReducer and useContext for global state?

blocks.text: Put the reducer in a top-level provider and share state and dispatch through context. This creates a lightweight Redux-like store without extra libraries. Splitting state and dispatch into two contexts avoids re-rendering components that only dispatch.

title: What does useMemo do?

blocks.text: useMemo(calculate, deps) caches the result of an expensive calculation and recomputes it only when dependencies change. It can also keep object or array references stable so memoized children or effect dependencies don't change unnecessarily. Use it for real performance problems, not for every value.

title: What does useCallback do?

blocks.text: useCallback(fn, deps) returns the same function reference between renders until dependencies change. Functions are re-created on every render, which breaks React.memo on children that receive them as props, or causes effects that depend on them to re-run. useCallback(fn, deps) is equivalent to useMemo(() => fn, deps).

title: What is the difference between useMemo and useCallback?

blocks.text: • useMemo memoizes the result of calling a function (a value).
• useCallback memoizes the function itself.
• Both take a dependency array and are used to preserve referential equality or avoid expensive work.
• With the React Compiler (stable since late 2025), much of this manual memoization is done automatically.

const total = useMemo(() => cart.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price, 0), [cart]);  // value
const handleAdd = useCallback(item => setCart(c => [...c, item]), []);       // function

title: When should you NOT use useMemo or useCallback?

blocks.text: Memoization has its own cost: storing values, comparing dependencies and added code complexity. Avoid it for cheap calculations, for functions passed only to native DOM elements, or when the child is not memoized anyway. Measure with the React Profiler first; optimize only real bottlenecks. If your project uses the React Compiler, manual memoization is rarely needed.

title: What are custom hooks?

blocks.text: A custom hook is a JavaScript function whose name starts with "use" and which calls other hooks. It lets you extract and reuse stateful logic (not state itself) across components. Each component calling the hook gets its own independent state.

title: Write a custom hook for fetching data.

blocks.text: A useFetch hook encapsulates loading, error and data states plus request cancellation, so components only consume the result.

title: Write a useDebounce custom hook.

blocks.text: Debouncing delays updating a value until the user stops changing it for a set time. It is commonly used for search inputs to avoid calling an API on every keystroke.

title: Write a useToggle and a useOnClickOutside hook.

blocks.text: These are small but very common interview hooks. useToggle simplifies boolean state; useOnClickOutside closes dropdowns or modals when the user clicks elsewhere.

title: What is useId?

blocks.text: useId generates a unique, stable ID that is consistent between server and client rendering. It is used to connect labels and inputs or ARIA attributes. Do not use it for list keys.

title: What is useTransition?

blocks.text: useTransition marks a state update as a non-urgent "transition". React keeps the UI responsive by rendering urgent updates (typing, clicking) first and interrupting the transition if needed. It returns [isPending, startTransition]. In React 19, startTransition can also accept async functions ("Actions").

title: What is useDeferredValue?

blocks.text: useDeferredValue(value) returns a version of the value that may lag behind during urgent updates. React first re-renders with the old deferred value, then renders again in the background with the new value. It is ideal when you do not control the state setter, e.g. deferring a slow list that depends on a fast-changing input.

title: What is the difference between useTransition and useDeferredValue?

blocks.text: • useTransition wraps the state update; you need access to the setter.
• useDeferredValue wraps a value; useful when the value comes from props or a parent.
• useTransition gives an isPending flag; with useDeferredValue you compare the value and deferred value yourself.
• Both use the same concurrent rendering mechanism and neither delays with a fixed timeout like debouncing.

startTransition(() => setFilter(value));  // control the update
const deferred = useDeferredValue(filter); // control the value

title: What is useSyncExternalStore?

blocks.text: useSyncExternalStore(subscribe, getSnapshot, getServerSnapshot?) lets components subscribe to external stores (browser APIs, third-party state libraries) safely under concurrent rendering, avoiding "tearing" where different parts of the UI show different values. State libraries like Redux and Zustand use it internally.

title: What is the use() hook in React 19?

blocks.text: use(resource) reads the value of a Promise or a Context. When given a Promise, the component suspends until it resolves, showing the nearest Suspense fallback; if it rejects, the nearest error boundary shows. Unlike other hooks, use can be called inside conditions and loops. The promise should be created outside the component (e.g. passed from a server component or cached) so it is not recreated every render.

title: What is useActionState?

blocks.text: useActionState (React 19, formerly useFormState) manages state returned from an action, typically a form submission. It returns [state, formAction, isPending]. The action receives the previous state and the form data, and its return value becomes the new state.

title: What is useFormStatus?

blocks.text: useFormStatus (from react-dom) gives a component information about the parent form's last submission: pending, data, method and action. It must be called from a component rendered inside a <form>, which makes it ideal for reusable submit buttons.

title: What is useOptimistic?

blocks.text: useOptimistic shows a temporary, optimistic version of state while an async action is in progress, so the UI feels instant. When the action finishes, React replaces the optimistic state with the real state; if it fails, the optimistic value is discarded.

title: What is useDebugValue?

blocks.text: useDebugValue adds a label to a custom hook in React DevTools, making it easier to inspect. It has no effect on behaviour. You can pass a formatting function to defer expensive formatting until the hook is inspected.

title: What is a stale closure in React hooks?

blocks.text: A stale closure happens when a function (inside an effect, timer or callback) captures a state or prop value from an earlier render and keeps using that old value. It often occurs when dependencies are missing from useEffect or useCallback. Fixes: include dependencies, use the updater form of setState, or store the latest value in a ref.

title: How do you mimic componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate and componentWillUnmount with hooks?

blocks.text: • componentDidMount: useEffect with an empty dependency array.
• componentDidUpdate: useEffect with dependencies (optionally skip the first run with a ref).
• componentWillUnmount: return a cleanup function from an effect with [].
Hooks encourage thinking in terms of synchronization rather than lifecycle moments.

title: Why does my useEffect run twice in development?

blocks.text: In React 18+ under StrictMode, React intentionally mounts, unmounts and re-mounts every component once in development. This stress-tests that your effects have correct cleanup. It does not happen in production. The fix is to implement cleanup properly, not to remove StrictMode.

title: How do you avoid infinite loops with useEffect?

blocks.text: Infinite loops happen when an effect updates state that is also one of its dependencies, or when a dependency is a new object/function on every render. Fixes: remove unnecessary dependencies by computing values during render, use the updater form, memoize objects with useMemo, or move object creation inside the effect.

title: Do you always need useEffect? ("You Might Not Need an Effect")

blocks.text: No. Effects are for synchronizing with external systems. Many effects in real code are unnecessary and add extra renders. Do not use effects to: compute derived data (do it during render), reset state when a prop changes (use a key), or respond to user events (use event handlers).

title: How do you use multiple state variables vs a single state object?

blocks.text: Use separate useState calls for unrelated values; it keeps updates simple. Group values into one object (or useReducer) when they always change together, like x/y coordinates or form fields. Remember that object state is replaced, not merged, so spread the previous value.

title: How do you update nested state objects and arrays immutably?

blocks.text: Copy every level you change using spread syntax or array methods that return new arrays (map, filter, concat, slice). For deeply nested data, libraries like Immer let you write mutable-looking code that produces immutable updates.

title: How do you share logic between components without hooks? (Comparison)

blocks.text: Before hooks, logic reuse relied on Higher-Order Components (HOCs) and render props, which led to "wrapper hell" in DevTools and confusing prop origins. Custom hooks solve the same problem with plain function calls and no extra component layers, which is why they are now the preferred pattern.

title: How do you reset a component's state?

blocks.text: React preserves state as long as the component stays in the same position in the tree with the same type. To reset it, change its key. React then treats it as a new component, unmounting the old one and mounting a fresh one with initial state.

title: Can you use hooks inside class components?

blocks.text: No. Hooks only work in function components and custom hooks. To use hook-based logic in an existing class component, wrap it in a function component (or HOC) that calls the hook and passes the result as props.

title: What are the lifecycle phases of a class component?

blocks.text: A class component goes through three phases:
• Mounting: constructor, static getDerivedStateFromProps, render, componentDidMount.
• Updating: static getDerivedStateFromProps, shouldComponentUpdate, render, getSnapshotBeforeUpdate, componentDidUpdate.
• Unmounting: componentWillUnmount.
Additionally, error handling uses static getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch.

title: What is the purpose of the constructor in a class component?

blocks.text: The constructor runs before mounting. It is used to initialize this.state and bind event handler methods. You must call super(props) first so that this.props is available. With class field syntax, you can usually skip the constructor entirely.

title: Why do we need to bind event handlers in class components?

blocks.text: In JavaScript, class methods are not bound to the instance automatically. When a method is passed as a callback (onClick={this.handleClick}), it loses its "this" context, so this is undefined in strict mode. Bind in the constructor, use arrow function class fields, or use an inline arrow function.

title: How does setState work in class components?

blocks.text: this.setState(updater, callback) schedules an update and shallow-merges the new object into existing state (unlike useState, which replaces). It can take an object or a function (prevState, props) => partialState. The optional callback runs after the update is applied and the component re-rendered.

title: What is componentDidMount used for?

blocks.text: componentDidMount runs once after the component is inserted into the DOM. It is the place for side effects that need the DOM or should happen once: fetching data, adding subscriptions, setting timers or integrating third-party libraries.

title: What is componentDidUpdate and how do you avoid infinite loops in it?

blocks.text: componentDidUpdate(prevProps, prevState, snapshot) runs after every update (not on initial mount). It is used to react to prop or state changes, such as refetching data when an ID changes. Always compare with previous values before calling setState, otherwise each update triggers another update.

title: What is componentWillUnmount used for?

blocks.text: componentWillUnmount runs right before the component is removed from the DOM. Use it to clean up: clear timers, cancel network requests, remove event listeners and unsubscribe from stores. Calling setState here is pointless because the component will never re-render.

title: What is shouldComponentUpdate?

blocks.text: shouldComponentUpdate(nextProps, nextState) lets a class component skip re-rendering by returning false. It is a performance optimization; by default it returns true. React.PureComponent implements it with a shallow comparison of props and state.

title: What is getDerivedStateFromProps?

blocks.text: static getDerivedStateFromProps(props, state) runs before every render and returns an object to update state, or null. It exists for rare cases where state must depend on prop changes over time. Because it is static, it cannot access "this". Most uses are better replaced by computing values during render, memoization, or resetting with a key.

title: What is getSnapshotBeforeUpdate?

blocks.text: getSnapshotBeforeUpdate(prevProps, prevState) runs right before DOM changes are committed. It lets you capture information from the DOM (like scroll position), and its return value is passed as the third argument to componentDidUpdate. It is commonly used for chat windows that keep scroll position when new messages arrive. There is no hook equivalent yet.

title: What are error boundaries?

blocks.text: Error boundaries are class components that catch JavaScript errors anywhere in their child tree during rendering, in lifecycle methods and in constructors. They display a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app. They implement static getDerivedStateFromError (to render fallback) and/or componentDidCatch (to log errors). They do not catch errors in event handlers, async code (setTimeout, promises) or server rendering.
Interview tip: The react-error-boundary package provides a ready-made function-friendly ErrorBoundary with reset support.

title: How do you handle errors in event handlers and async code?

blocks.text: Since error boundaries do not catch these, use regular try/catch and store the error in state to show feedback. To forward an async error to an error boundary, you can set state with a function that throws during render.

title: What is React.createRef and how is it different from useRef?

blocks.text: createRef creates a new ref object each time it is called, so it is used in class components (assigned once to an instance field). useRef returns the same ref object on every render and is used in function components. Using createRef in a function component would create a new ref every render.

title: Which lifecycle methods are deprecated (UNSAFE_)?

blocks.text: componentWillMount, componentWillReceiveProps and componentWillUpdate are legacy and renamed with an UNSAFE_ prefix. They often caused bugs with async rendering because they could run multiple times before commit. Replacements: use the constructor or componentDidMount instead of componentWillMount; getDerivedStateFromProps or componentDidUpdate instead of componentWillReceiveProps; getSnapshotBeforeUpdate instead of componentWillUpdate.

title: What is forceUpdate?

blocks.text: forceUpdate() forces a class component to re-render, skipping shouldComponentUpdate. It is rarely needed and usually signals reading data from outside React state. In function components, the equivalent trick is a dummy reducer, but useSyncExternalStore is the proper solution for external data.

title: What is a Higher-Order Component (HOC)?

blocks.text: A HOC is a function that takes a component and returns a new enhanced component. It is a pattern for reusing logic such as authentication checks, logging or data injection. Examples include React-Redux's old connect() and withRouter. Today custom hooks are generally preferred, but HOCs still appear in many codebases.

title: What are the drawbacks of HOCs?

blocks.text: • Wrapper hell: many nested wrappers in DevTools.
• Prop name collisions: two HOCs may inject the same prop name.
• Unclear data origin: it's hard to see which HOC provided a prop.
• Static methods and refs aren't passed through automatically (need hoist-non-react-statics and ref forwarding).
• Must not be applied inside render, or the component remounts every render.

title: What is the render props pattern?

blocks.text: A render prop is a prop whose value is a function that returns JSX. The component calls this function with its internal data, letting the consumer decide what to render. It shares logic while giving full rendering control. The children-as-a-function variant is common.

title: What is the compound components pattern?

blocks.text: Compound components are a group of components that work together and share implicit state through context, giving users a flexible, expressive API. Examples: <Tabs>, <Tabs.List>, <Tabs.Tab>, <Tabs.Panel>, or <select> and <option> in HTML.

title: What is the Container/Presentational pattern?

blocks.text: This pattern separates components into containers, which handle data fetching and state logic, and presentational components, which only receive props and render UI. It improves reusability and testability. With hooks, the "container" logic often moves into custom hooks instead.

title: What is component composition and why is it preferred over inheritance?

blocks.text: Composition means building complex components by combining simpler ones, passing components as children or props. React recommends composition over inheritance because it is more flexible and avoids deep class hierarchies. Meta reports never needing component inheritance hierarchies in its codebase.

title: What is the Context API and when should you use it?

blocks.text: Context provides a way to pass data through the tree without props at every level. Create it with createContext, provide a value with a Provider, and read it with useContext. It suits "global" data that many components need and that changes infrequently: theme, locale, authenticated user, feature flags. For frequently changing, complex state, a dedicated store may perform better.

title: What are the performance pitfalls of Context?

blocks.text: Every component that calls useContext re-renders whenever the provider's value changes. If you pass a new object every render (value={{ user, setUser }}), all consumers re-render even if nothing changed. Solutions: memoize the value, split contexts by concern (state vs dispatch), keep fast-changing state local, or use a selector-based store like Zustand.

title: What are Portals in React?

blocks.text: Portals render children into a DOM node outside the parent component's DOM hierarchy, using createPortal(child, container). They are used for modals, tooltips, toasts and dropdowns that must escape overflow:hidden or z-index stacking. Events still bubble through the React tree, not the DOM tree.

title: What is Suspense?

blocks.text: Suspense lets you show a fallback (like a spinner) while some part of the tree is not ready. Components "suspend" when they are waiting for lazy-loaded code (React.lazy), data read with use(), or Suspense-enabled data libraries. Suspense boundaries can be nested to reveal content progressively, and on the server they enable streaming HTML.

title: What is code splitting and how do you do it with React.lazy?

blocks.text: Code splitting breaks the JavaScript bundle into smaller chunks loaded on demand, reducing initial load time. React.lazy(() => import("./X")) defines a component whose code loads the first time it renders; it must be wrapped in Suspense. Route-based splitting is the most effective place to start.
Interview tip: React.lazy requires a default export. For named exports: lazy(() => import("./X").then(m => ({ default: m.Named }))).

title: What is concurrent rendering?

blocks.text: Concurrent rendering (React 18+) allows React to prepare multiple versions of the UI at once and interrupt rendering work. Urgent updates (typing) can pre-empt non-urgent ones (rendering a big list). It powers useTransition, useDeferredValue, Suspense streaming and selective hydration. It is enabled automatically when you use createRoot and concurrent features.

title: What is hydration?

blocks.text: Hydration is the process where React attaches event handlers and state to HTML that was rendered on the server, making it interactive. React expects the client render to match the server HTML; mismatches cause warnings and re-rendering. hydrateRoot is the client API. React 18+ supports selective hydration, hydrating parts wrapped in Suspense independently.

title: What is the difference between CSR, SSR, SSG and ISR?

blocks.text: • CSR (Client-Side Rendering): the browser downloads JS and renders everything. Fast after load, weaker SEO and slower first paint.
• SSR (Server-Side Rendering): HTML is generated on each request on the server, then hydrated. Good SEO and first paint, more server load.
• SSG (Static Site Generation): HTML is built at build time. Very fast and cacheable, but data can be stale.
• ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration, Next.js): static pages regenerated in the background after a revalidation time.

title: What are React Server Components (RSC)?

blocks.text: Server Components run only on the server (at build time or per request). They can access databases and files directly and send their rendered output to the client, but their code is never shipped in the JS bundle. They cannot use state, effects or browser APIs. Client Components, marked with "use client", handle interactivity. Frameworks like Next.js App Router use Server Components by default.

title: What is the difference between Server Components and SSR?

blocks.text: SSR renders components (including client components) to HTML on the server for the initial load, but all that component code is still sent to the browser and hydrated. Server Components never hydrate and their code never reaches the browser; they produce a serialized tree that can be refetched without losing client state. They are complementary: frameworks use SSR to render the initial HTML of both kinds.

title: What are Server Actions / Server Functions?

blocks.text: Server Functions (marked with "use server") are async functions that run on the server but can be called from client code, most often as a form action. React handles the network request. They simplify mutations without writing separate API routes, and work with useActionState and progressive enhancement.

title: What are Actions in React 19?

blocks.text: Actions are async functions used in transitions, especially form submissions. React 19 lets you pass a function to <form action={fn}>; React manages pending state, errors, optimistic updates and resets the form on success. Related hooks are useActionState, useFormStatus and useOptimistic.

title: What other new features came in React 19?

blocks.text: • ref as a regular prop (no forwardRef needed) and cleanup functions for callback refs.
• <Context> can be used directly as a provider.
• Native support for document metadata: <title>, <meta> and <link> rendered anywhere are hoisted into <head>.
• Stylesheet support with precedence, and async script deduplication.
• Resource preloading APIs: preload, preinit, prefetchDNS, preconnect.
• Better hydration error messages and support for custom elements (Web Components).
• Removal of legacy APIs: ReactDOM.render, hydrate, string refs, propTypes checks, legacy context.
React 19.2 (late 2025) added <Activity> for hiding UI while preserving state and useEffectEvent for non-reactive logic inside effects.

title: What is the React Compiler?

blocks.text: The React Compiler (formerly "React Forget"), released as stable v1.0 in October 2025, is a build-time tool (Babel/SWC plugin) that automatically memoizes components and values. It analyzes your code and inserts the equivalent of useMemo, useCallback and React.memo where safe, so you write plain React and still avoid unnecessary re-renders. It relies on your code following the Rules of React.

title: What is useEffectEvent?

blocks.text: useEffectEvent (stable in React 19.2) creates an "effect event": a function that always sees the latest props and state but is not reactive, so it does not need to be in the effect's dependency array. It separates logic that should re-trigger an effect from logic that should merely read the latest values.

title: What is the <Activity> component?

blocks.text: <Activity mode="visible" | "hidden"> (React 19.2) lets you hide part of the UI while preserving its state and DOM. Hidden content is not shown, its effects are cleaned up, and its updates run at low priority. It is useful for tabs or back-navigation where you want to keep form input or scroll state, and for pre-rendering content the user is likely to visit.

title: How do events propagate in React and how does event delegation work?

blocks.text: React attaches a single listener per event type at the root container and dispatches synthetic events through the component tree (delegation). Events bubble up through React components just like in the DOM, including through portals. You can stop bubbling with e.stopPropagation() and listen in the capture phase with onClickCapture.

title: What are Web Components and can React use them?

blocks.text: Web Components are browser-native custom elements with encapsulated DOM (Shadow DOM). React can render them like normal tags. React 19 added full support: properties are set correctly and custom events can be listened to with on+EventName props.

title: What is the difference between a stateful and a stateless component?

blocks.text: A stateful component manages its own state (useState, useReducer, or this.state). A stateless component only renders based on props, making it simpler, more predictable and easier to test. A good architecture keeps most components stateless and lifts state to a few owners.

title: How does React preserve and reset state based on the component tree position?

blocks.text: React ties state to a component's position in the render tree. If the same component type renders at the same position, its state is preserved, even if props change. If a different type renders at that position, or the key changes, the state is destroyed. This explains why conditionally swapping identical components keeps their state.

title: What are the "Rules of React"?

blocks.text: • Components and hooks must be pure: same inputs give the same output; no side effects during render.
• Props and state are immutable snapshots: never mutate them directly.
• Values passed to hooks and JSX must not be mutated afterward.
• React calls components and hooks: never call a component as a regular function or pass hooks around as values.
• Follow the Rules of Hooks (top-level only, React functions only).
These rules let React and the React Compiler safely optimize, re-render and run concurrently.

title: What causes a React component to re-render?

blocks.text: A component re-renders when: its own state changes, its parent re-renders (by default all children re-render too), or a context it consumes changes. Changing props alone does not cause a re-render; props change because the parent re-rendered. Rendering does not always mean the DOM changes; React only commits differences.

title: What is React.memo?

blocks.text: React.memo(Component, arePropsEqual?) is a higher-order component that skips re-rendering a function component when its props are shallowly equal to the previous props. It helps when a component renders often with the same props and its render is expensive. A custom comparison function can be provided.
Interview tip: Memo fails if you pass new objects, arrays or inline functions each render; combine it with useMemo/useCallback or the React Compiler.

title: How do you optimize the performance of a React application?

blocks.text: • Avoid unnecessary re-renders: React.memo, useMemo, useCallback, or enable the React Compiler.
• Keep state as local as possible; move state down to the components that need it.
• Code-split with React.lazy and dynamic import; lazy-load images.
• Virtualize long lists (react-window, TanStack Virtual).
• Use useTransition/useDeferredValue for heavy UI updates.
• Debounce or throttle expensive handlers.
• Use production builds and analyze bundle size; tree-shake large libraries.
• Use SSR/SSG or Server Components for faster first load.
• Measure first with React DevTools Profiler and Lighthouse.

title: What is list virtualization (windowing)?

blocks.text: Virtualization renders only the visible items of a long list, plus a small buffer, instead of thousands of DOM nodes. As the user scrolls, items are recycled. It dramatically reduces DOM size and render time. Popular libraries are react-window, react-virtuoso and TanStack Virtual.

title: How do you use the React DevTools Profiler?

blocks.text: The Profiler tab in React DevTools records renders while you interact with the app. It shows a flame graph of which components rendered, why they rendered ("Why did this render?" setting), and how long each took. You can also use the <Profiler> component in code to measure render timing programmatically.

title: What is debouncing and throttling, and how do you apply them in React?

blocks.text: Debouncing waits until events stop for a set time before running a function (e.g. search input). Throttling runs a function at most once per interval (e.g. scroll or resize handlers). In React, keep the debounced/throttled function stable across renders with useMemo or useRef, and cancel it on unmount.

title: Why is defining components inside other components bad for performance?

blocks.text: A component defined inside another component's body is a new function on every render. React sees a different component type each time, so it unmounts and remounts the inner component, losing its state and DOM and costing performance. Always define components at the top level.

title: How do inline functions and objects in JSX affect performance?

blocks.text: Inline arrow functions and object literals create new references on each render. For normal DOM elements this is cheap and fine. It only matters when passing them to memoized children or using them as effect dependencies, where the new reference defeats memoization. Then use useCallback/useMemo or the React Compiler.

title: How do you lazy load images in React?

blocks.text: Use the native loading="lazy" attribute so the browser defers off-screen images. For more control (placeholders, fade-in), use the Intersection Observer API in a custom hook or component. Also provide width and height to avoid layout shift.

title: What are Web Vitals and how does React relate to them?

blocks.text: Core Web Vitals are Google's user-experience metrics: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint, loading), INP (Interaction to Next Paint, responsiveness) and CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift, visual stability). React apps improve LCP with SSR/SSG and code splitting, improve INP with transitions and fewer re-renders, and reduce CLS by reserving space for images and async content.

title: What is React Router?

blocks.text: React Router is the most popular routing library for React. It maps URLs to components, enabling navigation in single-page apps without full page reloads. Version 7 can be used as a simple library (BrowserRouter, Routes, Route) or as a full framework with loaders, actions and SSR (successor to Remix).

title: What is the difference between Link, NavLink and an anchor tag?

blocks.text: An <a href> tag triggers a full page reload, losing app state. <Link to> performs client-side navigation by updating the URL with the History API. <NavLink> is a Link that knows if it is active, letting you style the current page link.

title: How do you read URL parameters and query strings in React Router?

blocks.text: Use useParams for dynamic route segments (like :id) and useSearchParams for query strings (?sort=price).

title: How do you navigate programmatically?

blocks.text: Use the useNavigate hook, which returns a function to change routes from event handlers or effects. You can pass state, replace history entries, or go back with navigate(-1). Inside render, use the <Navigate> component instead.

title: What are nested routes and Outlet?

blocks.text: Nested routes let child routes render inside a parent layout. The parent component renders <Outlet />, where the matched child route appears. This is ideal for layouts with shared headers or sidebars. An index route renders at the parent's exact path.

title: How do you create protected (private) routes?

blocks.text: Wrap routes that require authentication in a component that checks the user and redirects to login if not authenticated, often remembering where the user wanted to go.

title: What are loaders and actions in React Router?

blocks.text: In data/framework mode, a loader fetches data before a route renders, and an action handles mutations from <Form> submissions. This removes "fetch in useEffect" waterfalls, since data loading starts in parallel with navigation, and React Router revalidates loaders automatically after actions.

title: What is the difference between BrowserRouter and HashRouter?

blocks.text: BrowserRouter uses clean URLs (/about) based on the HTML5 History API; the server must be configured to return index.html for all routes. HashRouter stores the route after a # (/#/about); the server never sees the path, so it works on static hosts without configuration, but URLs are less clean and worse for SEO.

<BrowserRouter><App /></BrowserRouter>   // example.com/about
<HashRouter><App /></HashRouter>         // example.com/#/about

title: What is Redux and what are its core principles?

blocks.text: Redux is a predictable state container. Its principles are: a single source of truth (one store), state is read-only (changed only by dispatching actions), and changes are made with pure reducer functions. Redux Toolkit (RTK) is the official, recommended way to write Redux today, reducing boilerplate.

title: How do you connect React components to Redux?

blocks.text: Wrap the app in <Provider store={store}>, then read state with useSelector and dispatch actions with useDispatch. useSelector only re-renders the component when the selected value changes.

title: What is the Redux data flow?

blocks.text: 1) The UI dispatches an action (a plain object with a type). 2) The store calls the reducer with the current state and the action. 3) The reducer returns new state. 4) The store notifies subscribers, and components using useSelector re-render if their selected data changed. Middleware sits between dispatch and the reducer to handle side effects.

title: What is middleware in Redux, and what are thunks?

blocks.text: Middleware intercepts actions before they reach reducers to add capabilities such as logging, async logic or analytics. A thunk is a function dispatched instead of an object; the thunk middleware (included in RTK) calls it with dispatch and getState, enabling async work. createAsyncThunk generates pending/fulfilled/rejected actions automatically.

title: What is RTK Query?

blocks.text: RTK Query is the data fetching and caching tool built into Redux Toolkit. You define endpoints once, and it generates hooks that handle loading state, caching, deduplication, polling and cache invalidation through tags.

title: Context API vs Redux: when should you use which?

blocks.text: • Context is built-in and ideal for low-frequency global values (theme, auth, locale). It is not a state manager itself; it just passes values down.
• Redux (Toolkit) suits large apps with complex, frequently updated shared state, needing DevTools time-travel, middleware and strict patterns.
• With Context, every consumer re-renders on value change; Redux's useSelector re-renders only components whose selected slice changed.
• For server data, use a server-state library (TanStack Query, RTK Query) rather than either.

title: What is Zustand?

blocks.text: Zustand is a small, hook-based state management library. You create a store with a function, and components select only the parts they need, re-rendering only when those parts change. No providers or boilerplate are required, which makes it a popular lightweight alternative to Redux.

title: What is the difference between server state and client state?

blocks.text: Client state is owned by the browser: UI toggles, form inputs, selected tabs. Server state lives on a remote server and is only cached on the client; it can become stale, needs refetching, deduplication and synchronization. Libraries like TanStack Query and SWR specialize in server state, while useState, Context, Zustand or Redux handle client state.

title: What is derived state and why should you avoid duplicating state?

blocks.text: Derived state is any value that can be computed from existing props or state. Storing it separately in state creates two sources of truth that can get out of sync. Compute it during render instead (with useMemo if expensive).

title: How do you handle form validation in React?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: For simple forms, validate in the change or submit handler and store errors in state. For larger forms, libraries such as React Hook Form (with schema validators like Zod or Yup) or Formik reduce boilerplate. Also use native HTML validation attributes (required, type="email", minLength) for accessibility.

title: How do you test React components?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: The standard stack is Jest or Vitest as the test runner with React Testing Library (RTL). RTL encourages testing behaviour the way users interact: find elements by role, label or text, fire events with user-event, and assert on what appears. Avoid testing implementation details such as internal state.

title: What is the difference between getBy, queryBy and findBy in React Testing Library?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: • getBy...: returns the element or throws if not found; use for elements that should be present.
• queryBy...: returns null if not found; use to assert something is absent.
• findBy...: returns a Promise that resolves when the element appears (async, retries up to a timeout); use for elements that appear after data loads.
Each has an All variant (getAllBy, etc.) for multiple elements.

title: How do you mock API calls in tests?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: Mock fetch or modules with jest.fn()/vi.fn(), or better, use Mock Service Worker (MSW), which intercepts network requests at the network level so components use real fetch code. Then assert on the rendered result with findBy queries.

title: How do you test custom hooks?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: Use renderHook from React Testing Library. It renders the hook inside a test component and returns result.current. Wrap state updates in act() so React processes them before assertions.

title: What is snapshot testing?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: Snapshot testing saves the rendered output of a component to a file and compares future renders against it. Any difference fails the test until the snapshot is reviewed and updated. Snapshots catch unintended UI changes but can become noisy; use them sparingly, mainly for small stable components.

title: How do you use TypeScript with React components?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: Type props with an interface or type alias. Hooks infer types from initial values, or you can pass generics. Event handlers use React event types. Use React.ReactNode for children.

title: How do you create a generic component in TypeScript?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: Generic components accept a type parameter so they work with any data type while keeping type safety, for example a reusable List or Select.

title: How do you type useReducer and Context in TypeScript?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: Use a discriminated union for actions so TypeScript narrows the payload in each case. For context, type the value and either provide a default or allow null with a guard hook.

title: How do you make React apps accessible?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: • Use semantic HTML (button, nav, main, label) rather than clickable divs.
• Link labels to inputs (htmlFor + id, use useId).
• Provide alt text for images and aria-* attributes where semantics are missing.
• Manage focus for modals and route changes; trap focus inside dialogs.
• Ensure keyboard support (Tab, Enter, Escape) and sufficient color contrast.
• Test with eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y, axe and screen readers.

title: What are common security concerns in React applications?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: • XSS: React escapes values by default, but dangerouslySetInnerHTML, javascript: URLs in href, and injecting user data into scripts are risks; sanitize with DOMPurify.
• Sensitive data: never put secrets or API keys in frontend code; everything in the bundle is public.
• Auth tokens: prefer httpOnly secure cookies over localStorage to reduce token theft through XSS.
• Dependencies: audit npm packages regularly.
• Server Components/Functions: validate inputs and authorize every server action, since they are public endpoints.

title: How do you manage environment variables in a React app?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: Build tools inject environment variables at build time. In Vite, variables must start with VITE_ and are accessed via import.meta.env; in Next.js, browser-exposed ones start with NEXT_PUBLIC_. These values end up in the public bundle, so only non-secret configuration belongs there.

title: How should you structure a large React project?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: There is no single official structure, but feature-based organization scales well: group components, hooks, API calls, and tests by feature or domain rather than by file type. Keep shared UI components and utilities in common folders, and use absolute imports or path aliases.

src/
  app/            # app setup, routes, providers
  features/
    auth/         # LoginForm.jsx, useAuth.js, authApi.js, auth.test.jsx
    cart/
    products/
  components/     # shared UI: Button, Modal, Spinner
  hooks/          # shared hooks
  lib/            # api client, utils
  styles/

title: What are some React best practices interviewers look for?
category:
Forms, Testing, TypeScript and
Best Practices

blocks.text: • Keep components small and focused; extract custom hooks for logic.
• Keep state minimal and close to where it is used; derive instead of duplicating.
• Use stable unique keys; never mutate state.
• Clean up effects; avoid unnecessary effects.
• Prefer composition and TypeScript for safety.
• Handle loading, empty and error states.
• Use error boundaries and Suspense boundaries thoughtfully.
• Write behaviour-focused tests and follow accessibility guidelines.

title: Build a Todo app with add, toggle and delete.

blocks.text: This classic question tests state, lists, keys, events and immutable updates.

title: Build a search filter for a list.

blocks.text: Keep only the query in state and derive the filtered list during render.

title: Implement pagination for data fetched from an API.

blocks.text: Store the current page in state and include it in the effect's dependencies or query key. Disable navigation at the boundaries.

title: Build an infinite scroll list.

blocks.text: Use an IntersectionObserver on a sentinel element at the bottom of the list. When it becomes visible, load the next page and append results.

title: Build a reusable Modal component with Escape-to-close.

blocks.text: Combine a portal, an effect for the keydown listener, and children for content.

title: Build an accordion where only one panel is open at a time.

blocks.text: Lift the "open index" state to the parent so panels coordinate.

title: Build a countdown timer with start, pause and reset.

blocks.text: Store remaining seconds in state and the interval ID in a ref. Clean up on unmount and stop at zero.

title: Build a dark/light theme toggle that persists.

blocks.text: Combine context for global access, localStorage for persistence, and a data attribute on the root element for CSS.

title: Build a star rating component.

blocks.text: This tests controlled props, hover state and accessibility.

title: Build a multi-step form wizard.

blocks.text: Keep the current step index and the accumulated form data in the parent. Each step receives data and an update function.

title: Implement a shopping cart with quantity and total.

blocks.text: Use useReducer for cart actions and derive totals during render.

title: What is the output? Explain the batching behaviour.

blocks.text: This tricky question tests understanding of state snapshots and the updater function.

title: Find the bug: why does the count never go above 1?

blocks.text: The interval callback captures count from the first render (a stale closure) and the empty dependency array prevents the effect from re-running. Use the updater form so React supplies the latest value.

title: Build a "select all" checkbox list.

blocks.text: The header checkbox is derived from the items' state: checked when all are selected, and indeterminate when only some are. The indeterminate property must be set through a ref because it has no HTML attribute.

title: Build a toast notification system using context.

blocks.text: A provider keeps a list of toasts and exposes a function to show one. Each toast removes itself after a timeout. Any component can trigger a toast through a custom hook.

title: Find the performance problem: why does the whole list re-render while typing?

blocks.text: The text state lives in the same component as the expensive list, so every keystroke re-renders all rows. In addition, a new onSelect function is created every render, which would defeat React.memo. Fix it by moving the input state into its own component and memoizing the row and its callback (or by enabling the React Compiler).
